qt: to the Commission Nela Riehl (Verts/ALE), Damian Boeselager (Verts/ALE), Anna Strolenberg (Verts/ALE), Kai Tegethoff (Verts/ALE), Cecilia Strada (S&D), Mélissa Camara (Verts/ALE), Jaume Asens Llodrà (Verts/ALE), Reinier Van Lanschot (Verts/ALE), Rudi Kennes (The Left), David Cormand (Verts/ALE), Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE), Catarina Vieira (Verts/ALE), Chloé Ridel (S&D), Hanna Gedin (The Left), Kim Van Sparrentak (Verts/ALE), Krzysztof Śmiszek (S&D), Vladimir Prebilič (Verts/ALE), Annalisa Corrado (S&D), Tineke Strik (Verts/ALE), Matjaž Nemec (S&D), Robert Biedroń (S&D), Leila Chaibi (The Left), Gerben-Jan Gerbrandy (Renew), Mounir Satouri (Verts/ALE), Benedetta Scuderi (Verts/ALE), Kira Marie Peter-Hansen (Verts/ALE), Villy Søvndal (Verts/ALE), Abir Al-Sahlani (Renew), Manon Aubry (The Left), Marc Botenga (The Left), Thijs Reuten (S&D), Irene Montero (The Left), Sara Matthieu (Verts/ALE), Rima Hassan (The Left), Hana Jalloul Muro (S&D), Rasmus Nordqvist (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Recent cases have shown financial and digital service providers to have denied services to EU citizens targeted by extraterritorial US sanctions – namely UN Special Rapporteur Albanese and International Criminal Court Judge Guillou – as a result of compliance concerns. In both cases, access to essential banking and payment services in the EU was restricted despite the individuals operating legally under EU jurisdiction. Such practices are contrary to EU law and undermine fundamental principles such as judicial independence, multilateral accountability and financial sovereignty. They also raise questions about EU payment service obligations, including continuity of service in the internal market. In this context: 1.

How does the Commission assess the implications of such cases for the integrity of EU law, the independence of international institutions, and the EU’s ability to protect citizens from extraterritorial foreign sanctions?

Does the Commission intend to reinforce the enforcement of the EU Blocking Statute and provide short-term tools (including EU-backed protected payment channels), while supporting EU-based financial and payment providers through growth opportunities and regulatory incentives to reduce dependence on non-EU payment infrastructures?

Will the Commission engage diplomatically at UN level and with the United States to ensure extraterritorial measures do not hinder the EU’s ability to safeguard its financial and digital sovereignty and protect EU citizens and EU-supported institutions from foreign coercive measures?
This question is supported by Members other than the authors: César Luena (S&D), Jonas Sjöstedt (The Left).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.2.2026) The Commission deeply regrets the recourse to US sanctions that place undue pressure on the International Criminal Court (ICC) and those working for or cooperating with it. Furthermore, the threat of secondary sanctions directed at EU operators for engaging in certain activities with the targets of existing sanctions, regardless of any direct link to the sanctioning country, constitutes an extra-territorial application of sanctions that the Commission considers contrary to international law and opposes, including in UN fora. In EU statements at UN level, notably when addressing false notions of ‘unilateral coercive measures’ put forward against EU autonomous restrictive measures, the EU systematically underlines that sanctions must comply with the UN Charter, international humanitarian law and due process. The EU consistently raises concerns when third country measures risk undermining the integrity of the multilateral system, the functioning of EU backed institutions or the protection of humanitarian and legitimate economic activities. The Commission continues its close monitoring of developments related to the imposition of US sanctions affecting the ICC and those associated with its work. It remains in close contact with the ICC, the Member States and relevant stakeholders, and reiterates the importance of safeguarding the independence and functioning of the ICC. The Commission continues to stand ready to provide its full support to safeguard the ICC against external pressure and to assess appropriate and effective measures to ensure that the ICC’s operations remain unaffected and that its mandate is fully upheld.
